papers.title: Operating a bistable qubit
papers.abstract: Parasitic two-level-system (TLS) defects limit the stability and performance of solid-state quantum processors. Their interaction with a qubit can cause discrete, stochastic shifts of the qubit frequency, making the qubit bistable. We experimentally demonstrate an adaptive protocol for operating a bistable qubit with high fidelity using a classical controller powered by a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). Our "1-bit feedback" protocol estimates the qubit's bistable frequency from only one single-shot measurement, reaching the information limit set by the qubit's intrinsic entropy. We validate the protocol in a superconducting qubit by suppressing TLS-induced Ramsey beating, and deploy it to stabilize gate fidelities over time with approximately 136 kHz estimation bandwidth and a 77% error reduction. Our approach provides a simple, yet fundamentally efficient strategy for mitigating dephasing errors induced by strongly coupled TLS defects, and may enable the operation of large future qubit arrays suffering from few remaining, discrete instabilities.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates a real-time adaptive feedback protocol for operating a superconducting transmon qubit that exhibits bistable frequency switching induced by a strongly coupled TLS defect. The 1-bit feedback scheme estimates which of two qubit frequency modes is active from a single optimally-timed measurement ($\tau_{\mathrm{opt}} \approx 1.33$ µs), then updates the control frequency accordingly to suppress dephasing and stabilize gate fidelities.
summary.motivation: Parasitic TLS defects in dielectrics of superconducting qubits cause telegraphic frequency fluctuations that degrade coherence and gate fidelity. While ensemble TLS noise has been addressed, strongly coupled individual TLSs inducing discrete bistable frequency shifts require active mitigation strategies that operate on the qubit coherence timescale.
summary.method: A TLS-syndrome circuit prepares the qubit in a superposition state calibrated for the high-frequency mode, evolves it for time $\tau_{\mathrm{opt}} = 1/(2\Delta_{\mathrm{TLS}})$ where $\Delta_{\mathrm{TLS}} \approx 374$ kHz, then applies an inverse pulse and measures in the Z basis. The single measurement outcome determines which mode is active; an FPGA-based controller (Quantum Machines OPX1000) uses this 1-bit feedback to update the drive frequency in real time with $\approx 136$ kHz bandwidth.
summary.result: Randomized benchmarking over 14 minutes shows native single-qubit gate infidelity reduces from $(1.4 \pm 1.1) \times 10^{-3}$ without feedback to $(0.65 \pm 0.18) \times 10^{-3}$ with feedback—a 77% error reduction—while suppressing TLS-induced Ramsey beating. The estimation error probability is $p_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 9\%$, well below the 25% utility threshold.

papers.title: Closed form logical error rate approximations for surface codes
papers.abstract: We propose a novel method to calculate logical error rates in surface codes, assuming independent and identically distributed physical errors. These results fit well known scaling laws for studied physical error rates and code distances, but break down in some other regimes. Increasing the code distance still reduces logical error rates, but returns diminish quickly beyond a certain point. We show how to use our method to analyze hypothetical quantum computers with various configurations and select designs with lower error rates. Currently, this requires expensive classical simulations of quantum decoders for various distances and physical error rates or inaccurate extrapolation from minimal experimental data. Instead, we use the symmetry of the problem to count the configurations that result in a logical error with our novel software. Given a physical error rate, we can deduce the probability of a logical error to provably good accuracy quickly. We include an analysis of measurement errors to allow for a more complete comparison of different surface code implementations. We extend this counting method to a particular locally-correlated error model and another globally-correlated error model.

summary.summary: This work develops a closed-form method to calculate logical error rates $L$ for surface codes by recursively counting minimum-length logical paths (MLLPs) containing $d_e = (d+1)/2$ errors, avoiding expensive decoder simulations. The approach proves accurate when $pd^2 \ll 1$ and provides rigorous bounds for the regime $pd^2 \gtrsim 1$, and is extended to locally and globally correlated error models plus measurement errors.
summary.motivation: Designing practical quantum computers requires rapidly evaluating logical error rates across many combinations of physical error rate $p$ and code distance $d$, but current methods rely on computationally prohibitive Monte Carlo simulations or inaccurate extrapolation from sparse experimental data.
summary.method: The authors exploit topological constraints of surface codes to enumerate error configurations via dynamic programming (Algorithm 1 with memoization), computing $C_{d_e}$ exactly for unrotated codes as $d\binom{d}{d_e}$ and for rotated codes via path-counting with geometric constraints from Theorem 2; results are combined with binomial probabilities in Equation~1 and bounded by Theorem 1 to achieve provably accurate $L$ estimates in polynomial runtime.
summary.result: For unrotated codes, $C_{d_e} \approx \frac{d_e}{\pi}4^{d_e}$ and logical error scaling matches $L \approx A(p/p_\mathrm{th})^{d_e}$ with $p_\mathrm{th} \approx 1.22 \times 10^{-2}$ ($R^2 = 1 - 6.3 \times 10^{-6}$); rotated codes achieve $p_\mathrm{th} \approx 7.3 \times 10^{-2}$ but require only $\approx 75\%$ of the qubits for equivalent fidelity.
